newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Albright to seek Jewish roots in Prague.
newsitem.headline: Albright to seek Jewish roots in Prague.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, who makes an emotional visit to the land of her birth on Sunday, plans to seek her Jewish family roots in Prague, U.S. officials said on Saturday.

Albright, visiting the Czech Republic for the first time since becoming Secretary of State, is to go on Sunday evening to Prague's ancient Jewish cemetery and to look for the names of her grandparents, who died in the Holocaust, on the walls of a synagogue, a U.S. official travelling with her said.

Revelations about Albright's origins caused a stir in February when the Washington Post, researching her background, found she appeared to be of Jewish ancestry and that three of her grandparents had died in the Holocaust.
"This has been an intensely personal issue for her. She has tried not to let it interfere with her work but now she has the opportunity to...learn more about it," the U.S. official said.
Albright, who speaks Czech, was born Marie Jana Korbelova in Prague in 1937. Her father, Josef Korbel, was a Czechoslovak diplomat.

The names of her paternal grandparents, Arnost Korbel and his wife Olga, are listed on the memorial wall of the Pinkas Synagogue, dedicated to Czechoslovak Jews deported to concentration camps during World War Two.
Albright also plans to look at documents at Prague's Jewish Town Hall, the centre of the old Jewish quarter.
A White House spokesman said when the Post reports emerged that Albright had believed she was Roman Catholic and was only now coming to understand her heritage was Jewish.
Albright, on a whirlwind tour of Eastern Europe, arrived in St Petersburg on Saturday for talks with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov on NATO expansion and arms control.
She is due in Prague on Sunday after a stop in Lithuania.

Albright is due to meet Czech Foreign Minister Josef Zieleniec to discuss NATO's invitation this week to the Czech Republic to join the alliance. She will also have a private dinner with President Vaclav Havel.

After this week's NATO summit in Madrid, Albright said she was pleased with the invitations to Poland and Hungary but the call to the Czech Republic had warmed her heart. "It makes me feel that I've been part of history," she said.
Zieleniec told a news conference on Friday Albright's visit would be an important stage in the process of negotiations towards NATO membership.
But beyond affairs of state, Albright's visit is a homecoming. She still has a cousin in the Czech Republic but it was not clear whether they would meet.
However, she is scheduled to walk on Monday from the palatial Foreign Ministry, where her father used to work, to Prague Castle and will pass the house where she lived as a small girl.
Prague has long seen Albright as a powerful friend.
On Monday, she is to receive the Order of the White Lion, the highest Czech civilian honour.
Albright's family fled the former Czechoslovakia twice, once to escape the Nazis and then, in 1948, the communists.
Her father served with the World War Two government-in-exile in London and was later given political asylum in the United States, where he settled with his family.
She will also deliver a speech at Prague's art deco Municipal House, recently restored to its original splendour.
As an academic, Albright advised Havel, a former dissident playwright, after the 1989 "Velvet Revolution" which ended 40 years of communism in Czechoslovakia.
Later, as U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, she joined Havel in a smoky Prague jazz club to hear U.S. President Bill Clinton play the saxophone during a 1995 state visit.
